blocks.text: Class Weighting offered a genuinely clean, data preserving fix, but it still required retraining the model with a different internal configuration. Threshold tuning, the final topic in this module, requires genuinely no retraining at all, it works entirely after training is already complete, simply changing how an already trained model predicted probabilities get converted into a final class decision.

This topic covers what the default classification threshold actually is, why 0.5 is genuinely often a poor, arbitrary fit for an imbalanced problem, how lowering or raising that threshold trades off recall against precision for the minority class, how a precision recall curve helps choose a genuinely better threshold, and why this technique combines freely with every other technique covered throughout this entire module.
1. The Default Classification Threshold

blocks.alt: A predicted probability passes a 0.5 threshold into a class decision

blocks.text: Most classification models genuinely output a predicted probability, not a direct class label, a value between 0 and 1 representing how confident the model is that a row belongs to the positive class. By default, that probability is genuinely compared against a threshold of 0.5, at or above becomes a positive prediction, below becomes negative.

This default threshold is genuinely built into most classification workflows without much thought, exactly the assumption this topic exists to question directly for the specific, real case of an imbalanced classification problem.
2. Why 0.5 Is Genuinely Often the Wrong Choice

blocks.alt: Imbalanced data often makes the default 0.5 threshold wrong

blocks.text: A threshold of exactly 0.5 is genuinely just an arbitrary midpoint, it carries no actual connection to the real, practical cost of a false positive versus a false negative for a specific, real problem. Missing a genuinely real fraud case might be considerably more costly in practice than incorrectly flagging one legitimate transaction, yet 0.5 treats both kinds of mistake as equally acceptable by default.

This mismatch matters genuinely more for imbalanced problems specifically, a model trained on genuinely rare positive examples often produces predicted probabilities that rarely even reach 0.5 for real positive cases, quietly causing the model to miss most of them under the default threshold, even when it has genuinely learned something real and useful about the pattern.

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: A threshold of 0.5 is genuinely a default, not a rule. For an imbalanced problem specifically, it is worth treating as just one candidate among several, not an automatic, correct choice.

blocks.text: 3. Lowering the Threshold: More Recall, Less Precision

blocks.alt: A lower threshold produces more recall but less precision

blocks.text: Genuinely lowering the threshold, say to 0.3, means the model now flags a row as positive with less confidence required, catching genuinely more real minority cases that would have fallen just below 0.5 before. This comes with a genuine tradeoff, more legitimate, negative cases now also cross that lower bar, producing genuinely more false positives.

This tradeoff, genuinely more recall at the cost of genuinely lower precision, is often exactly the right direction for problems where missing a real positive case, a fraud, a disease, a failure, is considerably more costly than a false alarm.
4. Raising the Threshold: More Precision, Less Recall

blocks.alt: A higher threshold produces more precision but less recall

blocks.text: Genuinely raising the threshold, say to 0.7, requires more confidence before flagging a row as positive, reducing genuinely false positives, since only the clearest, most confident cases get flagged at all. The real cost runs the opposite direction, genuinely more real minority cases now fall below that higher bar and get missed entirely.

This direction genuinely makes sense when a false positive is considerably more costly or disruptive than a missed case, flagging too many legitimate transactions as fraud, for instance, when each flag triggers a genuinely expensive manual review process.
5. A Worked Example

blocks.alt: A model output probability with a custom threshold of 0.3 produces better recall

blocks.text: Comparing predictions at two different thresholds on the same trained model predicted probabilities shows this tradeoff directly, with no retraining involved at all.

code.content:
import numpy as np

# Predicted probabilities from an already trained model
predicted_probabilities = np.array([0.12, 0.45, 0.55, 0.68, 0.31, 0.72, 0.49, 0.9])

default_predictions = (predicted_probabilities >= 0.5).astype(int)
lower_threshold_predictions = (predicted_probabilities >= 0.3).astype(int)

print("Default threshold 0.5:", default_predictions)
print("Lower threshold 0.3:", lower_threshold_predictions)

blocks.text: Notice that a value like 0.31 genuinely flips from negative under the default 0.5 threshold to positive under the lower 0.3 threshold, with genuinely no change to the model itself at all, only the decision rule applied to its existing predicted probabilities changed.

blocks.title: A practical habit
blocks.content: Always keep the raw predicted probabilities around, not just the final class labels. Threshold tuning genuinely requires access to those probabilities, and recomputing them later means rerunning the model unnecessarily.

blocks.text: 6. Choosing a Genuinely Better Threshold

blocks.alt: Trying several thresholds and checking the target metric picks the best one

blocks.text: Rather than guessing, a genuinely systematic approach tries several candidate thresholds and plots precision and recall at each one, producing a precision recall curve, a technique covered in real depth in the Model Evaluation Classification module later in this course. That curve makes the genuine, real tradeoff visible directly, letting a specific threshold be chosen based on which balance of precision and recall actually fits the real, practical costs of the problem at hand.

This is genuinely the correct way to select a threshold, rather than assuming 0.5 by default, or arbitrarily picking another single number, the precision recall curve shows the genuine, full range of tradeoffs available, letting an informed, deliberate choice be made instead.

blocks.text: 7. Why This Combines Freely With Everything Else in This Module

Threshold tuning genuinely operates entirely at prediction time, after a model has already been trained, whether that training used under sampling, over sampling, SMOTE, ADASYN, class weighting, or none of them at all. It genuinely does not care how the model got its predicted probabilities, only that it has them, which means it can genuinely be layered on top of any other technique covered in this module without conflict.

This makes threshold tuning genuinely worth applying almost by default, even after using one of the more involved techniques covered earlier in this module, it costs essentially nothing, requires no retraining, and can only genuinely help fine tune the final, real decision boundary a deployed model actually uses.

blocks.text: 8. Closing Out the Handling Imbalanced Data Module

blocks.alt: The Handling Imbalanced Data module is complete, Feature Selection comes next

blocks.text: This module covered a genuinely complete range of strategies for a real, common problem, a target class that is genuinely rare. Under sampling and over sampling addressed it by directly changing row counts, SMOTE and ADASYN improved on that by generating genuinely new, synthetic examples rather than exact duplicates, class weighting moved the fix into the algorithm itself, and threshold tuning, covered here, applies the genuinely simplest, final adjustment at prediction time.

With features now genuinely encoded, scaled, and imbalance properly addressed, the next module, Feature Selection, addresses a genuinely different, final preparation question, given every feature now available, which ones actually earn their place in a final model, and which are genuinely better left out.

items: The default classification threshold, 0.5, is genuinely arbitrary and often a poor fit for an imbalanced problem.
Lowering the threshold genuinely increases recall, catching more real minority cases, at the cost of more false positives.
Raising the threshold genuinely increases precision, fewer false positives, at the cost of missing more real cases.
A precision recall curve helps choose a genuinely better threshold based on real, practical costs.
Threshold tuning requires genuinely no retraining, applied entirely at prediction time on existing probabilities.
It combines freely with every other technique in this module, since it operates independently of how the model was trained.
